title: Who leads Marburg virus research? Gender, geography and funding in authorship, 2008 to early 2023: a bibliometric baseline before the 2023-2025 outbreaks
abstract: Between 2023 and 2025, Marburg virus disease reached Equatorial Guinea, Tanzania, Rwanda and Ethiopia for the first time. WHO's 2025 Marburg research priorities make leadership of studies by local scientists a continuing goal. This study describes who led Marburg virus research before these outbreaks. I analysed 684 English-language Web of Science papers on Marburg virus published from 2008 to February 2023 (5,700 authorships). Gender was inferred from first names with Gender-API, papers about African countries were identified from their text, funders were harmonised by country and type, and themes were mapped to the WHO priorities. I used Wilson 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and logistic and negative binomial regression. Women held 35.1% (95% CI 33.9-36.4) of authorships, 41.6% (37.9-45.4) of first-author and 19.6% (16.7-22.9) of last-author positions. Women last authors rose from 15.1% (2008-2012) to 23.2% (2018-2023). Only 14.6% of papers had an author based in Africa. Of 102 papers about an African country, 25.5% (18.0-34.7) had a first author and 23.5% (16.4-32.6) a last author from that country, below benchmarks for infectious-disease research in Africa. Women based in Africa were last author on 2 papers. Of funded papers, 69.0% acknowledged a US funder (24.0% a US defence agency) and 3.2% an African funder. WHO priorities on clinical care, outbreak trials, social science and capacity strengthening each appeared in fewer than 8% of papers. An apparent citation penalty for funded papers disappeared after adjustment (rate ratio 1.07, 0.87-1.33). Before the recent outbreaks, Marburg virus research was led mostly by men in senior positions and by researchers outside the affected countries, and was funded mainly by US agencies. This baseline can track whether recent African-led responses change who leads the field.

title: Cross-reactive antibody and functional T-cell responses to Bundibugyo virus induced by Zaire ebolavirus vaccination and infection
abstract: Background There is no licensed specific vaccine against the current Ebola Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) outbeak affecting the Democratic Republic of the Congo. However, clinical evaluations of a licensed Zaire ebolavirus (EBOV) vaccine have just launched. It remains unclear whether EBOV infection or vaccination generate cross-reactive immunity against BDBV. Methods We quantified CD4 and CD8 T-cell magnitude, polyfunctionality, and cytotoxicity after 8-day expansion with EBOV, BDBV, Sudan (SUDV), or Marburg (MARV) GP peptide pools, and measured GP-binding antibodies by multiplex assay, in recipients of Ad26.ZEBOV/MVA-BN-Filo (n=10), single-dose rVSVG-ZEBOV-GP (n=10), or two-dose rVSVG-ZEBOV-GP (n=8) (NCT02876328), and in EVD survivors sampled approximately 3 years after infection (n=10). Findings Fourteen days after completion of each licensed vaccine regimen, median BDBV-reactive CD4 responses were 9.8% [IQR:8.9-14.0] after single-dose rVSVG-ZEBOV-GP (D14) and 8.0% [5.5-9.9] after Ad26.ZEBOV/MVA-BN-Filo (D70). The highest BDBV-reactive CD8response was observed in survivors (24.7% [20.3-33.1]), together with a prominent cytotoxic CD8 response (14.4% [10.4-19.7]) ; corresponding vaccine-group medians ranged from 0.9% to 17.7% and from 0.6% to 6.7%, respectively. SUDV responses were also detected, whereas MARV recognition was limited. BDBV-binding antibodies were detected following both vaccine regimens, with the highest levels observed in survivors (491 [330-1261] net MFI). Among vaccinees, EBOV- and BDBV-reactive cellular and humoral responses were positively correlated after adjustment for multiple testing. Interpretation EBOV infection and vaccination elicited BDBV-cross-reactive T-cell responses and binding antibodies. These findings support further evaluation of existing EBOV vaccines in the context of BDBV outbreaks. Funding INSERM, Vaccine Research Institute (ANR-10-LABX-77-01), and Institut de Recherche pour le Developpement (IRD).

title: Mechanism of Action Studies of Small Molecule Entry Inhibitors Targeting Filovirus Glycoproteins
abstract: Ebola virus (EBOV) and Marburg virus (MARV) are highly pathogenic filoviruses. Infection with either of these viruses results in viral hemorrhagic fever (VHF), a severe disease that can lead to multiorgan failure, internal bleeding, and, oftentimes, death. Currently, no antivirals are approved for the treatment of filoviruses, underscoring the urgent need for broad-spectrum antivirals. Currently, two vaccines are FDA-approved against EBOV disease; however, they are only effective against EBOV Zaire, while recent EBOV outbreaks have been caused by EBOV Sudan, underscoring the need for broad-spectrum vaccines and antivirals. Thus, our research goal is to develop small molecule inhibitors that directly target the filoviral glycoprotein (GP), which mediates viral entry into host cells for both EBOV and MARV. Our study is divided into two chapters: the development of broad-spectrum anti-filoviral entry inhibitors and the elucidation of the mechanisms of action (MOAs) of novel small molecule entry inhibitors.

title: The Attenuation Paradox in Bundibugyo Virus Disease: Case Fatality, Ascertainment, and Delayed Outbreak Recognition
abstract: Bundibugyo virus has caused three recognised outbreaks, and each was recognised late. The usual reading of that record treats the delay as a failure of investment, diagnostics or governance. This review sets out a partly mechanistic alternative: the low case fatality ratio observed early in a Bundibugyo virus outbreak is itself one of the conditions that produces the delay, and the delay in turn depresses the observed ratio further. The evidence is organised around three comparison tables: the burden, severity and recognition interval of each outbreak; the presenting clinical features set against a matched Ebola virus series; and the point at which species assignment failed in each event. A schematic draws the relationships together. Two findings emerge. The clinical syndrome does not discriminate between species: haemorrhage was documented in roughly a quarter of confirmed patients in both the 2007–08 Bundibugyo series and a 2014 Ebola virus series, so the presenting picture cannot carry the explanatory weight often placed on it. The discriminating failures are instead genomic and diagnostic, and the early case fatality ratio operates as a surveillance trigger that is biased downward precisely when ascertainment is narrowest. The 2026 epidemic, in which the confirmed ratio rose from 12.1% to 44.3% while the virus doubled every 5.5 days, fits this account better than it fits a change in virulence. A fatality ratio from the first weeks of a filovirus outbreak should therefore be read as an index of surveillance maturity rather than of danger, and escalation should be governed by species-inclusive confirmation.

title: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Public Health Science Priorities for the 2026 Ebola Outbreak Caused by Bundibugyo Virus
abstract: The ongoing 2026 Ebola outbreak is growing faster than any previous outbreak of Ebola disease. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) initiated an emergency response on May 17, 2026, to help respond to this outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Incorporating CDC’s principles for public health emergency response, a science agenda was developed during May through July to detail scientific priorities and key questions guiding agency response activities. The science agenda identifies 7 priority areas for CDC: epidemiology, surveillance, and modeling; laboratory diagnostics and genomics; risk communication and community engagement; prevention and mitigation strategies; medical countermeasures; transmission, natural history, and ecology; and situational awareness and preparedness. For each of these priority areas, the agenda provides brief contextual information and articulates scientific questions and considerations. This agenda is intended to shape expectations about where CDC scientific expertise and activities could make impactful public health contributions to the control of this outbreak. Science questions are prioritized for this initial stage of the outbreak and focus on evidence needed for guiding outbreak control activities. Future iterations could incorporate external partner feedback.

title: C-Terminal Dimerization Enables Assembly of Ebola Virus VP30 Oligomers with transcriptional support activity.
abstract: Ebola virus VP30 is a multifunctional phosphoprotein essential for initiating viral transcription. VP30 functions as a homo-oligomer, where oligomerization is critical for its transcriptional-support activity. While a tetra-leucine motif in the N-terminal region (amino acids (aa) 100-105) mediates oligomerization, the structural determinants and functional relevance of a VP30 dimerization motif in the C-terminus remained poorly defined. Using a novel high-resolution (1.43 Å) crystal structure and biochemical approaches, we identified residues 142ITLL145 in the VP30 C-terminal domain (CTD) as key contributors to VP30 dimerization. Alanine conversions of these residues (VP30-CTD142-145A) disrupted CTD dimerization, as demonstrated by native mass spectrometry, size-exclusion chromatography with multi-angle light scattering, and split-GFP complementation assays. Notably, VP30-CTD functions as a dominant-negative inhibitor of full-length VP30 in a minigenome assay, whereas the dimerization-deficient mutant VP30-CTD142-145A does not. Critically, introduction of these mutations into full-length VP30 completely abolished viral transcription in minigenome assays. Recombinant EBOV carrying the VP30 dimerization mutations could not be rescued in cell culture, demonstrating that VP30-CTD dimerization is essential for viral replication. Together, these findings establish that CTD-mediated dimerization is essential for VP30's transcriptional support activity and virus propagation, identifying VP30 dimerization as a previously uncharacterized determinant of the viral replication cycle. Importantly, the dimerization interface is conserved among filoviruses, suggesting it represents a broadly conserved and potentially targetable vulnerability for antiviral intervention.

title: The welfare and productivity losses associated with the death of an index case of Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Disease reported in Kenya on 6 October 2026
abstract: Abstract Introduction: Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease (EBVD) was imported into Kenya from the Democratic Republic of the Congo on 3 October 2026. Economic evidence is lacking to inform Kenya’s Ministry of Health’s advocacy for domestic and external investment to bolster prevention, mitigation, preparedness, and response to EBVD. This study aimed to estimate, from an economy-wide (societal) perspective, the discounted welfare and productivity losses associated with the death of the index case of EBVD in Kenya on 6 October 2026. Methods Drawing on various secondary sources, this study uses the human capital approach (HCA), the willingness-to-pay small (WTP_S) and large (WTP_L) models, and the willingness-to-accept small (WTA_S) and large (WTA_L) models to estimate discounted welfare and productivity losses associated with the death of the index case of EBVD in Kenya. To assess the robustness of the results, the five models were each re-estimated four times, assuming (i) a 5% discount rate, (ii) a 10% discount rate, (iii) Africa’s highest male average life expectancy at birth, 74.55 years in Tunisia, and (iv) the world’s highest male average life expectancy, 84.78 years in Monaco. Results Under the HCA model, the death of the 40-year-old male patient is expected to result in a total welfare loss of Int$120,944 and a productivity loss of Int$40,763. Using the implied WTP approach, the expected welfare loss would be between Int$423,302 and Int$786,133, with a productivity loss of between Int$142,669 and Int$264,957. Applying the implied WTA approach yields a welfare loss of Int$1,269,907 to Int$4,051,608 and a productivity loss of Int$428,007 to Int$1,365,546. Re-estimating the HCA, WTP_S, WTP_L, WTA_S, and WTA_L models with 5% and 10% discount rates reduced the estimated welfare and productivity losses by about 17% and 45%, respectively. Re-running the welfare and productivity loss models with Africa's and the world’s highest male life expectancies increased the welfare loss estimates by about 35% and 54%, respectively. Conclusions The death of the index case of EBVD in Kenya will likely lead to significant welfare and productivity losses. Kenya’s Ministry of Health should continue advocacy with the whole-of-government, the private sector, civil society, and development partners to urgently increase investment to bridge gaps in International Health Regulations core capacities, universal health coverage, and WASH (water, sanitation, and hygiene), thereby mitigating the risk of EBVD becoming a national epidemic.

title: Measurement Error Correction and Multidimensional Aggregation in Epidemiological Surveillance Systems: Application to the Ebola Virus Disease Epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
abstract: Epidemiological surveillance systems produce decision-making indicators from data that may be affected by under-reporting, misclassification and notification delays. These errors can propagate through the extraction, transformation, loading and multidimensional aggregation stages. This article proposes a mathematical framework that integrates measurement error correction into an ETL–data warehouse–OLAP decision architecture. The central problem is to determine whether the correction of a misclassification error can be performed before or after aggregation without changing the resulting indicator. We show that the Rogan–Gladen estimator commutes with the roll-up operator only when the sensitivity and specificity parameters are homogeneous across the aggregated strata. A numerical instantiation based on a synthetic dataset calibrated on published parameters of the Ebola virus disease epidemic in North Kivu and Ituri (DRC, 2018–2020) illustrates this non-commutation and its consequences for the estimation of incidence and the reproduction number. These results lead to a design rule: when surveillance quality is heterogeneous, correction must be performed at the finest level at which the error parameters can be regarded as homogeneous, before any aggregation, because this is the only strategy that remains unbiased whatever the spatial distribution of cases. A bias–variance analysis (Theorem 4) and a Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis (5,000 replicates, seven scenarios) further show that aggregate-level correction can have a slightly smaller variance but becomes biased when cases concentrate in poorly covered zones, and that the corrected indicators are highly sensitive to the assumed specificity when test positivity is close to the false-positive floor (a misspecification of 0.005 in specificity changes cumulative incidence by more than 100%). No individual-level surveillance data were used: the synthetic data are fully specified by a generation algorithm and a parameter table provided for reproducibility. The proposed framework thus provides a formal basis for designing surveillance decision-support systems that explicitly account for data quality.

title: Private healthcare facilities’ participation in Uganda’s viral hemorrhagic fever surveillance program: contributions, selective case capture, and underutilized early-warning potential
abstract: Abstract Background Private healthcare facilities are important initial points of contact, especially for patients with undifferentiated febrile illnesses in mixed health systems. However, their contribution to viral hemorrhagic fever surveillance remains to be quantified, particularly in outbreak-prone regions. We assessed their contribution to Uganda’s national surveillance system and examined variation by case mix, geography, and outbreak period. Methods We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional analysis of all suspected VHF specimen submissions recorded in Uganda’s national Result Dispatch System from 1 January 2023 to 14 August 2026, spanning the 2025 Sudan virus disease and 2026 Ebola (Bundibugyo virus, BDBV) outbreaks. Ownership was classified against the national health facility master list. Pre-specified outcomes were test positivity, recorded bleeding, and alive-at-reporting status. Adjusted analyses used generalized linear mixed models with a district-level random intercept, pre-specified sensitivity analyses, and a test of effect modification by Kampala. Results Of 7,929 submissions, 504 (6.4%) were private. Private healthcare facilities contributed 21 of 149 VHF-positive submissions and 10 of 32 Ebola-positive submissions. During May–June 2026, they contributed 212 of 1,230 submissions and 10 of 20 Ebola-positive submissions; Ebola positivity was 4.72% versus 0.98% in public submissions (post-hoc comparison; crude odds ratio 4.99, p = 0.0007). Private ownership was associated with overall VHF positivity (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 3.44, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.95–6.05), recorded bleeding (4.97, 3.86–6.41), and alive-at-reporting status among known-status records (5.43, 4.09–7.21). Positivity attenuated after reporting-status adjustment (2.40, 1.34–4.28); intervals included 1 in alive-only and pre-2026 analyses. Bleeding remained associated after adjustment for symptom recording (3.85, 2.98–4.97). The alive-at-reporting association was stronger in Kampala but remained elevated elsewhere. All 16 initially significant symptom comparisons remained significant after false discovery rate adjustment. Conclusions Private healthcare facilities contributed a small share of submissions but a disproportionate share of detections, recorded VHF-compatible bleeding far more often, and far more often reported patients still alive, unlike the post-mortem case-finding dominating public submissions in the capital. This is consistent with an underused early-warning role and supports targeted, differentiated integration; establishing any effect on timeliness requires prospective study. Trial registration Clinical trial number: not applicable.

title: In silico cyclic-minipeptides predicting antibody-free early-diagnosis of Ebola virus
abstract: In this work, in silico cyclic-minipeptide candidates were computationally generated aiming to develop antibody-free sandwichbased early-diagnosis of ebola virus (EBOV). Presently there are few approved early-rapid EBOV diagnosis, despite many antibody-based efforts. Cyclic-minipeptides were chosen here because i) their vast sequence numbers facilitate designs fitting the diagnostic sensibility and specificity requirements, ii) they are easy and cheaper to scale-up for production, and iii) their rigidity could be more resistant to denaturing-buffers for EBOV early disinfection during assay. In this work, the earlier most abundant biomarker for EBOV infections soluble glycoprotein sGP were computationally targeted. Hundreds of ~ 100-1000-fold 9- and 12-mer candidates predicting higher affinities than previously reported antibodies were proposed here combining Boltzgen/ Prodigy with our newly developed evolutionary-mutations. By targeting complementary sGP cavities with cyclic-minipeptide candidates, possible sandwich-pairs would still require experimentally-guided explorations. Additional computational screening work may also be possible to select the best candidates for possible pan-EBOV diagnosis.

title: Tetraspanin CD81 restricts Ebola virus infection and is antagonized by glycoprotein GP and matrix protein VP40
abstract: Viruses manipulate host cell membranes to evade antiviral immunity, prevent superinfection, and optimize their replication and spread. The Ebola virus glycoprotein GP mediates viral entry but also contributes to the subversion of host antiviral immune responses. Here, we characterize the impact of Ebola virus GP on cell surface proteins and show that it reduces cell surface availability of tetraspanins CD81, CD63, and CD9. This function is conserved among several filoviral glycoproteins but not observed for glycoproteins of other viral families. Whereas CD63 and CD9 are largely dispensable for Ebola virus replication, CD81 suppresses virus-like particle entry and viral replication. This activity might be attributed to CD81-mediated suppression of NF-κB signaling, which is induced by the Ebola virus matrix protein VP40 and transcription- and replication-competent virus-like particle (trVLP) replication. Our results further indicate that both GP, which interacts directly with CD81, and VP40, which also associates with CD81, function to reduce total and surface expression levels of CD81. CD81 is shown to reduce levels of Ebola virus RNA species, and its antibody-mediated clustering can suppress Ebola virus infection. Our study provides insights into the roles of NF-κB signaling in Ebola virus replication and immunopathogenesis, and identifies tetraspanin CD81 as a potentially druggable Ebola virus-inhibitory host factor.

title: Quantifying the extinction probability of Marburg virus disease outbreaks: A continuous-time Markov chain model integrating a multi-type branching process
abstract: Understanding the extinction dynamics of Marburg virus disease is crucial, particularly during the early stages of an outbreak when stochastic effects strongly influence disease outcomes. Although deterministic models have provided valuable insights into virus transmission dynamics, they cannot adequately capture random transmission events or quantify extinction probabilities, particularly when outbreaks begin with few infected cases. This study develops a continuous-time Markov chain stochastic model derived from a deterministic multi-host transmission model. The model incorporates a multi-type branching process, in which distinct infectious types are tracked according to their contributions to secondary infections, enabling estimation of disease extinction probabilities during the early outbreak phase. The extinction analysis shows that outbreaks initiated by exposed humans have a higher probability of extinction (21.6%) compared with those initiated by infectious humans (13.7%), whereas outbreaks initiated by infected bats have an extinction probability of only 0.36%, highlighting their role as important reservoirs sustaining virus transmission. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that reducing human-to-human transmission, decreasing viral shedding, and increasing environmental viral decay significantly enhance the likelihood of disease extinction. The proposed framework provides a quantitative tool for assessing Marburg virus disease outbreak risk and valuable insights for designing early interventions for human transmission, environmental contamination, and cross-species interactions.

full_text: Fourth, fifth, sixth and seventh meetings of the WHO Technical Advisory Group on candidate vaccine prioritization (TAG-CVP) for Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak response: meetings report, 1 September, 19 October, 22 October and 2 November 2026 Other Titles Abstract This meeting report summarizes the deliberations and recommendations of the WHO Technical Advisory Group on Candidate Vaccine Prioritization (TAG–CVP) following four meetings held between September and November 2026 in response to the Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern in May 2026. The Group reviewed evidence on two Bundibugyo virus-specific vaccine candidates, ChAdOx1 BDBV (University of Oxford) and mRNA-1469 (Moderna), to assess their suitability for clinical evaluation and outbreak response. The review covered preclinical toxicology, animal challenge studies, interim phase 1 safety and immunogenicity results, and vaccine manufacturing and availability. Both candidates demonstrated protection in ferret and non-human primate studies, induced antibody responses within 14 days and showed acceptable reactogenicity profiles in preliminary clinical trials. The Group also considered uncertainties concerning rare serious adverse events associated with the respective vaccine platforms. Based on the available safety, immunogenicity and protection data, TAG–CVP unanimously recommended including both candidates in the ongoing phase 2/3 clinical trial in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. analysis.main_results: The analysis of the outbreak samples suggested that the virus may have persisted in the host for a longer duration than previously thought, potentially allowing for prolonged transmission. This finding was based on the genetic and epidemiological data collected from the outbreak.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted these findings as evidence that Marburg virus might have a long-term hideout in the host, which could contribute to its transmission dynamics. This is a novel insight into the behavior of the virus during outbreaks.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings could inform future surveillance and diagnostic strategies for Marburg virus disease, helping to identify potential long-term viral persistence in hosts and improve outbreak response measures.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its focus on a single outbreak, which may not be representative of all Marburg virus transmission scenarios. However, the evidence is strong given the detailed genetic and epidemiological analysis conducted.

The findings are based on genetic and epidemiological data, offering a novel insight into the behavior of Marburg virus during outbreaks. While the study is limited to a single event, the evidence is robust and relevant for understanding the virus's transmission dynamics. The results could have important implications for public health measures and future research on Marburg virus disease.
